title: Prudential-HCL Venture Becomes India's Eighth Standalone Health Insurer and Starts Operations
summary: Prudential HCL Health Insurance received its IRDAI registration on July 1 and announced on August 20 that it has begun operations with an AI-enabled, direct-to-consumer model alongside agents.
description:
India's insurance regulator has registered a new standalone health insurer backed by the UK-listed Prudential plc and India's HCL Group. This article was first published in early August and has been updated on October 13, 2026 with the latest confirmed details, including the company's formal start of operations. According to Asia Insurance Post's report of July 1, the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India granted Prudential HCL Health Insurance Limited a Certificate of Registration to carry on health insurance business. That takes the number of standalone health insurers in India to eight and was the regulator's third new insurance registration of calendar 2026.

The ownership is a 70:30 joint venture. Prudential plc holds 70% through a subsidiary, and Vama Sundari Investments, the HCL Group vehicle, holds the remaining 30%. The venture was announced in March 2025, so the registration closes a process that took more than a year. Prudential has named Amit Dave as managing director and chief executive, described as CEO designate in the August announcement, and Abhishek Saraf as chief operating officer. The amount of capital invested has not been disclosed in the sources reviewed.

On August 20 Prudential announced that the insurer, which will operate as Prudential Health India, had commenced operations. The company describes a digital-first, service-led model aimed at making health insurance simpler to understand, buy and use. It plans an omnichannel approach that combines personal advice through an agency network with an AI-enabled direct-to-consumer platform, and it points to access to more than 12,000 hospitals, digital tools for choosing cover and managing policies, and preventive health and support services. The announcement did not name launch cities, list specific products or give prices, so potential customers should not expect a detailed product catalogue until the insurer files and markets its plans.

The market it is entering is large. Prudential cites the General Insurance Council of India as estimating that India's health insurance market produced about US$16 billion in gross written premium in fiscal 2026, and attributes demand to rising incomes, favourable demographics and growing awareness of health protection. Naveen Tahilyani, Prudential's regional chief executive for several Asian and African markets, described India as a strategically important market for the group. Amit Dave referred to the government's "Insurance for All by 2047" goal. Shikhar Malhotra of Vama Sundari said HCL's entry into health insurance is a natural extension of its capabilities. Prudential also said in May that it is seeking a 75% stake in Bharti Life, in addition to its existing life insurance and asset management joint ventures in India.

What is a standalone health insurer, and why does the category exist? In India, general insurers sell motor, property, travel and health policies together, while standalone health insurers are licensed to sell only health, personal accident and travel cover. Regulators created the category to encourage companies that specialise in health and to deepen penetration in a country where many households still pay for treatment out of pocket. The practical difference for consumers is focus: a standalone insurer has no motor or property portfolio to manage, and its entire performance depends on health claims, hospital relationships and customer service.

For a prospective buyer, a new insurer brings both opportunities and questions. On the positive side, new entrants often compete on service and technology, offer simpler policy documents and may provide features such as wellness rewards or digital claims tracking. They can also push established insurers to improve. On the other side, a new company has no claim settlement history, no track record on how it treats disputed claims and a hospital network that may still be growing. The 12,000-hospital figure is a company statement, and what matters to an individual is whether the hospitals near them are included for cashless treatment.

Before buying a plan from any health insurer, whether new or established, there are practical checks. Confirm the waiting periods for pre-existing conditions and specific procedures, because these differ widely between plans. Look at room-rent limits, co-payment clauses and sub-limits, which can reduce a payout even when the headline sum insured looks high. Check the claim settlement ratio and the number of days it takes to settle claims once the insurer has published them, and read the IRDAI disclosures that insurers are required to make. Ask about portability, which lets you move your policy to another insurer without losing accumulated benefits such as waiting-period credits. Finally, compare the premium with equivalent cover from at least two other insurers, since price differences for the same sum insured can be significant.

The entry also says something about where Indian insurance is heading. Regulators have been pushing for wider coverage and more competition, and global insurers are building local platforms rather than relying only on partnerships. If the Prudential-HCL venture delivers on its digital promises, customers could gain simpler onboarding and quicker claims. If it struggles, the lesson will be that distribution and hospital relationships are as important as technology. In either case, the first full year of reported numbers will show how quickly it can build a book of business.

For now, the confirmed facts are limited: the registration, the ownership, the leadership and the start of operations. Anything beyond that, including products, premium rates and claim performance, will become clear only as the insurer launches and files its plans. Readers considering a purchase should wait for official product documents and verify them on the company's website and IRDAI's public disclosures.

key_points: IRDAI granted Prudential HCL Health Insurance Limited a Certificate of Registration on July 1, 2026, making it India's eighth standalone health insurer and the regulator's third registration of the year.
Prudential plc holds 70% through a subsidiary and HCL Group's Vama Sundari Investments holds 30%; the joint venture was announced in March 2025.
On August 20, Prudential said the insurer had commenced operations, with a digital-first model combining agents and an AI-enabled direct-to-consumer platform.
The company cites a network of more than 12,000 hospitals and an Indian health insurance market of about US$16 billion in gross written premium in FY2026, per the General Insurance Council.
Amit Dave is the managing director and CEO designate; the insurer has not published product prices or the capital invested.
why_it_matters: Health insurance is one of the fastest-growing and most complained-about parts of Indian finance, so a new well-funded entrant can change choice, pricing and service. For buyers, a new insurer also means no track record on claims, so knowing what to check before buying matters more than the brand name.

title: UAE Central Bank Law Transition Ended on September 16: What Banks, Insurers and Fintechs Now Face
summary: The one-year grace period under Federal Decree-Law No. 6 of 2025 closed on September 16, and a law-firm newsletter reports the central bank granted no blanket extension; fines can reach AED 1 billion.
description:
The United Arab Emirates has moved from preparation to enforcement under its new central bank law. This article was first published in August, when financial institutions were counting down to a compliance deadline, and has been updated on October 13, 2026 now that the deadline has passed. Federal Decree-Law No. 6 of 2025, issued on September 8, 2025 and published in the Official Gazette on September 15, 2025, repeals the 2018 central bank law and the 2023 decree-law on insurance activities and replaces them with one framework covering banking, insurance, other licensed financial institutions and financial market infrastructure. According to law firm Ashurst, affected entities had until September 16, 2026 to comply, and the Central Bank of the UAE could extend the period.

The key question after September 16 is whether any relief was granted. A newsletter from the UAE firm CMI & Co dated October 2 says the one-year transitional period closed on that date, that the law became fully enforceable with no transitional relief, and that the central bank confirmed no blanket extension had been granted. The same newsletter says enforcement against non-compliant entities began immediately. This is a single secondary source, so firms should verify their own position directly with the central bank or its published circulars rather than relying on a law firm's summary.

The penalties explain why firms took the deadline seriously. Ashurst and Hadef & Partners both report maximum administrative fines of AED 1 billion for licensed financial institutions and up to AED 5 million for authorised individuals. CMI & Co adds that the previous maximum for institutions was AED 200 million, which would make the new cap five times larger, but that comparison comes from one source. Fines can be collected by debiting accounts held with the central bank or with any licensed institution, and the central bank may publish its enforcement decisions, including the name of the violator. Conducting licensed financial activity without a licence is a criminal offence carrying imprisonment and substantial fines, and Hadef notes that marketing or promoting licensed services without authorisation is itself a regulated activity.

The law also redraws the perimeter of regulation. It extends beyond open banking to regulated data sharing across products such as wealth management, insurance, pensions and credit scoring. Payment services that use virtual assets are licensable, although the law carves out investment holdings and certain swaps. Technology providers whose platforms, applications, protocols or infrastructure facilitate financial services may fall under the central bank's oversight even if they have no direct dealings with customers. CMI & Co says that under Article 62 fintech platforms, API providers, payment infrastructure operators, open finance providers and decentralised platforms must either be licensed or hold a documented central bank opinion confirming that they are out of scope, and warns of criminal liability risk for operating without that clarity.

For insurers, the stakes are specific. CMI & Co says the transitional alignment period for insurers has closed and that insurers must now comply fully with Articles 78 to 106 and the implementing instruments, which cover capital adequacy, governance including board composition, independent actuarial functions and internal audit, claims-handling service levels, fraud prevention and outsourcing. It adds that insurance compliance gaps are now assessed within the same supervisory and enforcement framework as banking breaches. Separately, in May the central bank issued a remuneration regulation for banks and insurers, which, according to Pinsent Masons, applies to insurance and reinsurance companies for the first time and requires independent review of pay frameworks at least every three years.

Consumers gain new protections. The law requires licensed institutions to run anti-fraud systems, including strong authentication and transaction monitoring, and to disclose products transparently. It creates a unified, independent complaints authority covering banking and insurance, and specialised judicial committees to resolve financial disputes of up to AED 100,000, with decisions in disputes of that size not open to challenge. Compound interest on customer credit facilities is prohibited. The law also gives the central bank early-intervention powers over distressed institutions, from remedial capital or liquidity measures to replacing management, facilitating mergers, imposing moratoria and liquidation. Other provisions recognise the Digital Dirham as legal tender and make environmental, social and governance principles part of the central bank's statutory functions.

What should firms do? The practical steps suggested by law firms are to assess licensing status and regulatory classification, update governance, risk management and consumer protection frameworks, review technology and fintech models, align operations with the digital asset and ESG provisions, and engage with the central bank early. Fintech and technology providers should check whether they sit within the perimeter, because the cost of getting that wrong has risen sharply. Firms operating through free zones or without proper authorisation face particular scrutiny, according to legal advisers.

For customers and policyholders in the UAE, the change should be gradual rather than dramatic. If you have a complaint with a bank or insurer, you should expect a more unified process in time, but you should check the central bank's current guidance for how to file one. If you use a fintech app or payment service, check that it is licensed. The law is a long text, and details such as implementing circulars continue to emerge, so this article should be read as a summary of reported provisions rather than legal advice. Firms and individuals with specific obligations should read the decree-law itself and take advice from a qualified UAE lawyer.
key_points: Federal Decree-Law No. 6 of 2025 was issued on September 8, 2025 and gazetted on September 15, 2025, replacing the 2018 central bank law and the 2023 insurance decree-law.
Affected firms had until September 16, 2026 to comply; the central bank could extend the period, and CMI & Co reports it confirmed that no blanket extension was granted.
Administrative fines can reach AED 1 billion for licensed institutions and AED 5 million for authorised individuals, and the central bank can publish violators' names and debit fines from accounts.
The law widens the regulatory perimeter to open finance, virtual-asset payment services and technology providers that facilitate financial services.
It creates a unified complaints authority for banking and insurance and specialised judicial committees for disputes of up to AED 100,000.
why_it_matters: Banks, insurers and fintechs operating in the UAE can no longer rely on transitional relief, and the penalties are large enough to affect boardroom priorities. Customers should also see a clearer route for complaints, while technology and fintech firms need to confirm whether they are now inside the regulator's perimeter.
